source.title: The Delta Learning Hypothesis: Preference Tuning on Weak Data can Yield Strong Gains
source.authors: Scott Geng; Hamish Ivison; Chun-liang Li; Maarten Sap; Jungshian Li; Ranjay Krishna; Pang Wei Koh

record.file_problem: The paper text is complete; the final pages include appendix material and figures.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a stronger model can improve from supervision produced by weaker models, but uses preference tuning on chosen/rejected pairs rather than the original weak-to-strong fine-tuning and PGR measurement.
record.gate_note: The study reports preference-tuning and SFT outcomes, including aggregate benchmark scores, a controlled style metric, and a logistic-regression theorem. It does not calculate PGR. It also reports results for individual benchmarks; selected task-level rows are retained where they illustrate variation. Results cited from other studies are not included.
record.test_reason: The study preference-tunes stronger 7–8B instruct/SFT models on pairs of outputs from weaker models (chosen: weak model; rejected: weaker model). It measures whether the student improves beyond its own baseline and beyond the chosen-response model, and compares this with SFT on the same weak outputs. That is a different method aimed at the same question as weak-to-strong generalization. Caveats: no PGR is computed, and the students already score at or above their weak supervisors before training. The Tülu 3 strong-supervision run (63.0) could serve as a ceiling, but the paper does not use it that way.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that the quality delta between paired weak responses can drive preference-tuning gains beyond either response, even when SFT on the weak data hurts. Their weak-data recipe matches Tülu 3 and OLMo 2 post-training, and they prove delta learning helps in logistic regression. Not all deltas work, gains saturate with chosen quality, and dependence on task and algorithm is left open.
record.recipe_differences: Uses preference optimization (primarily DPO) on chosen/rejected weak-model outputs rather than the original weak-label fine-tuning setup, and does not report PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with preference direction and delta size; the paper reports gains plateauing beyond approximately Δ ≈ 0.55, some large positive-delta pairs below the base-model reference, effects of chosen-response quality, and differences by benchmark. It also reports an exception in safety evaluation for Qwen 3B over 1.5B.

fits_no_version.finding: DPO on pairs where both models are much stronger than the student (Qwen 72B over 32B/14B) lowers the 8B student below its baseline. Chosen and rejected log-likelihoods both fall during training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Preference tuning on pairs from much stronger supervisors can hurt a weaker student (strong-to-weak failure of preference tuning).

fits_no_version.finding: Size-heuristic labels agree 80.5% with GPT-4o and give comparable downstream results (63.4 vs 62.9), except on AlpacaEval 2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weak heuristic preference labels can substitute for strong-judge labels in post-training.

record.problems: The authors describe the empirical study as limited in compute and based mainly on DPO, a few base models, and evaluations that do not cover all behaviors or domains. Several plotted results have no numerical values in the text. The paper reports choosing the best run across five seeds for its best setup, but does not provide uncertainty estimates for the main aggregate results.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports separate values for 11 benchmarks in Table 4, 8 benchmarks in Tables 1 and 3, and multiple individual Qwen model-pair results in Figure 3. These were not all transcribed as rows; aggregate rows and task-specific contrasts were prioritized. Other individual safety benchmark cells from Appendix Table A1 were omitted; selected aggregate safety rows and the stated exception are retained. Figure 4's plotted values are not numerically transcribed.

untested.parts: The PGR formula and a strong-ceiling comparison. Students that start below their supervisor on the task, as in Burns et al.'s base-model setup. UltraFeedback-Weak supervisor scores are not reported.
Auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling of weak supervisors, and PGR-scale method comparisons. Only DPO/SimPO vs SFT are tested.
Chess, reward modelling, internal representations, and systematic student-size scaling (students fixed at 7–8B).
All parts: exploitation of unverifiable supervisor errors, distribution shift, and correlated weak-strong errors.

missing.what: Qwen-1.5B-chosen outlier: positive gain but smaller than its delta predicts, conjectured because the chosen model is much weaker than the student
Theory predictions: expected gain grows with the teacher gap and shrinks with student strength. Numeric example: 80% student, 70%/60% teachers, d>2000, ≥90% of teacher pairs help
Strong-supervision reference (Tülu 3 data, 63.0) that would allow a PGR-like computation for r15–r17. Not done by the authors

record.verdict_notes: Main fixes: (1) r12–r14 used TruthfulQA cells as averages; the correct averages are 63.9/62.7/64.3/63.2. (2) r1/r3 cited 55.5 as the UltraFeedback-Weak supervisor score, but that is Llama-3B's Table 4 average. (3) r23/r24/r26 involve supervisors stronger than the student, so they are not weak-to-strong. The OLMo values are recoverable as 50.0→55.0 vs 54.8. V1 support is weak in kind: every student already matched or exceeded its supervisor before training, so 'beats the supervisor' needs no learning. The informative result is gain over the student's own baseline and over naive SFT, which maps better to V2. Best-of-5-seed selection for the top Tülu setup and the lack of uncertainty estimates weaken small differences such as +0.4 and +0.2.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not use Burns et al.'s PGR formula or report a PGR value. Its main tests use preference pairs, not fine-tuning solely on weak labels.
It compares DPO with SFT and tests SimPO and preference-label alternatives, but does not report PGR.
It examines language-model sizes, benchmark tasks, and some base models. It does not test chess or reward modelling, nor directly analyze internal representations.
No direct test of students exploiting what a supervisor cannot check, distribution shift, or gains shrinking when weak and strong models make similar errors.
The theory is for binary logistic regression with Gaussian inputs and specified assumptions, not a general guarantee for language models.

labels.reason: Sections 5.1–5.2 support dependence on delta magnitude and chosen-model quality, including saturation near Δ≈0.55. The 21-pair sweep includes supervisors stronger than the student and measures performance rather than PGR.

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.reason: Table A1 and Appendix C establish task-dependent costs: safety averages decline despite capability gains. These drops concern the initial student baseline; trained safety averages still exceed the respective chosen supervisors.

labels.label: supports
labels.condition: High-dimensional intercept-free logistic regression with Gaussian inputs, κ>0, specified step size/horizon
labels.reason: Theorem 6.1 guarantees alignment improvement under its conditions; Corollary 6.2 establishes that typical conditional-uniform teacher pairs satisfy the sufficient condition in high dimensions. Improvement also applies when the student initially exceeds both teachers.

relation.reason: The study directly compares preference training with weak-output SFT, evaluates students against supervisors and initial checkpoints, and proves conditions for improvement.

tranche.reason: Preference-pair training and logistic-regression analysis address learning beyond weak supervision using a different method and measure from the original weak-label/PGR setup.

source_check.notes: No PGR is reported; baseline-relative losses should not be read as failures to exceed supervisors. Appendix G.5 reports selection over five seeds for the best configuration without uncertainty intervals; the title page advertises a GitHub repository despite code=n in the pack.

statements.correction: Table 4: student baseline 57.2; chosen supervisors 55.5, 45.8, 57.5; DPO students 61.1, 59.3, 63.4 respectively. Qwen-3B supervisor exceeds the initial student by 0.3. SimPO reaches 62.4. No PGR or empirical uncertainty intervals reported.
statements.problem: The reported results are correct, but the blanket claim that the student already exceeded its supervisor is false for Qwen-3B.

statements.correction: Table 4: Tülu-3-8B-SFT baseline 57.2; Qwen-2.5-3B-Instruct supervisor 57.5; student after DPO 63.4. Table A3: student after SimPO 62.4. Preference-pair supervision; no PGR reported.
statements.problem: A student starting below its chosen supervisor is present, so this is not wholly untested in this study.

statements.correction: Section 3.2 and Table 3: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct baseline 63.9; SFT on its own greedy responses 62.7; DPO preferring its own responses over Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct responses 64.3. DPO gain over baseline +0.4; over SFT +1.6.
statements.problem: The cited r13 does not test DPO after weak-label SFT; its DPO and SFT conditions are separate training comparisons.
No explicit study-specific result is stated; cross-study counts and the aggregate status cannot be checked from this paper.

reader_labels.reason: Weak-response preference tuning improves the strong model's reported aggregate score; the Tülu weak-data rows also exceed the corresponding weak supervisor averages (r1, r3, r15-r17).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: DPO versus SFT on weak preference data; SimPO on the best weak preference dataset
reader_labels.reason: DPO improves while SFT on weak chosen responses degrades in the UltraFeedback-Weak experiments, and SimPO also yields gains (r1-r4, r21).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The positive-delta condition produces a large increase, but reversed and zero-delta controls do not; the outcome depends on preference direction and a meaningful delta (r9-r11).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Tülu weak-data post-training across tested model pairs and benchmarks
reader_labels.reason: All three weak-data setups improve average performance; the paper also reports a GSM8K increase for the Llama 3B-over-1B setup (r15-r18).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Changing delta magnitude, chosen-response quality, base model, and safety evaluation
reader_labels.reason: Delta-related gains plateau, some large positive-delta pairs hurt, gains depend on chosen-response quality and vary across tasks, and one weak-data model has a safety-evaluation decrease (r22-r29).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Specified high-dimensional binary logistic-regression setting with κ > 0
reader_labels.reason: The theorem guarantees an increase in alignment under its conditions, and the corollary gives a high-probability condition for most teacher pairs (r30).
